ideas.title: Same Stats, Different Graphs
ideas.description: Matejka and Fitzmaurice built the Datasaurus Dozen: twelve wildly different scatterplots that share the same mean, standard deviation, and correlation to two decimal places.

ideas.title: Anscombe's Quartet
ideas.description: A 1973 note thatshowed four datasets with the same means, variances, regression line, and R-squared, and four completely different stories once visualized.

ideas.title: Gender Shades
ideas.description: Buolamwini and Gebru audited three commercial gender-classification APIs and found error rates up to 34.7% for darker-skinned women versus 0.8% for lighter-skinned men (aggregated accuracy metrics had hid the discrepancies).

ideas.title: A Biased Health Care Algorithm
ideas.description: Obermeyer et al. showed that an algorithm used on millions of patients ''falsely concludes that Black patients are healthier than equally sick White patients'' (largely because it was based on predicting health costs).

ideas.title: Many Analysts, One Dataset
ideas.description: Silberzahn et al. gave 29 teams one dataset and one question — are soccer referees more likely to give red cards to dark-skinned players? Effect sizes ranged from 0.89 to 2.93; 20 teams found a significant effect and 9 did not.

ideas.title: The Parable of Google Flu
ideas.description: At its worst, Google Flu Trends overestimated doctor-visit rates by more than double

ideas.title: Sex Bias in Graduate Admissions
ideas.description: A canonical example of Simpson's paradox: Berkeley's 1973 admissions looked biased against women in aggregate, but the aggregate was driven by which departments women applied to.

ideas.title: Inherent Trade-Offs in Fair Risk Scores
ideas.description: Three common fairness conditions are mathematically incompatible.

ideas.title: Machine Bias (COMPAS)
ideas.description: ProPublica's investigation of the COMPAS risk score, and the parallel discussion around equal false-positive rates versus equal predictive value as validation tests.

ideas.title: Reproducibility in Psychology
ideas.description: 270 authors replicated 100 psychology studies. 97% of the originals reported significant results; 36% of the replications did, and mean effect sizes fell by about half.

ideas.title: Datasheets for Datasets
ideas.description: Gebru et al. propose a standard documentation record for datasets, based on datasheets for electronic components.

ideas.title: Model Cards for Model Reporting
ideas.description: Mitchell et al. propose short accompanying documents that report model performance, along with intended use and out-of-scope use.

ideas.title: The MusicLab Experiment
ideas.description: A classic. Salganik, Dodds, and Watts ran 14,341 participants through parallel artificial music markets. Songs in worlds that showed download counts became both more unequal and less predictable — the same song was a hit in one world and a flop in another.

ideas.title: The Vocabulary Problem
ideas.description: In this study, Furnas and colleagues analyzed spontaneous word choice for objects in five different contexts. They found the probability that two people would favor the same term for an object was less than 20%.

ideas.title: Algorithmic Amplification of Politics on Twitter
ideas.description: A rare 'counterfactual' audit, done from inside the company, in which millions of Twitter users were given reverse-chronological timelines instead of  algorithmically-ranked feeds.

ideas.title: Exposure to Diverse News on Facebook
ideas.description: Bakshy, Messing, and Adamic analyzed the 'filter bubble' into three stages for 10.1 million Facebook users: who your friends are, what the ranking algorithm shows you, and what you click.

ideas.title: Collaboration and Creativity: The Small World Problem
ideas.description: Uzzi and Spiro reconstructed the network of everyone who wrote, directed, choreographed, or produced a Broadway musical from 1945 to 1989. The relationship to artistic / financial success was an inverted U: with too little connection, good ideas never travel, but with too much, everyone converges.
ideas.source_label: Uzzi & Spiro, American Journal of Sociology, 2005

ideas.title: The Spread of True and False News Online
ideas.description: Vosoughi, Roy, and Aral tracked about 126,000 verified true and false stories as they moved through 3 million people on Twitter. False stories reached more people, spread faster, and went deeper into the network(s).

ideas.title: Can Cascades Be Predicted?
ideas.description: Given a cascade/domino/viral effect that has already reached size k, can you predict if it will reach 2k?
ideas.source_label: Cheng, Adamic, Dow, Kleinberg & Leskovec, WWW 2014

ideas.title: Systematic Inequality in Faculty Hiring
ideas.description: Clauset, Arbesman, and Larremore mapped 16,000 faculty placements as a directed network and recovered a steep prestige hierarchy: a quarter of institutions produce roughly 71–86% of all tenure-track faculty.

ideas.title: Asking About Social Circles
ideas.description: Galesic et al. improved election forecasts by asking respondents not only how they intended to vote, but also how the people around them would vote. The social-circle question was more effective than the own-intention question in US and French samples.
ideas.source_label: Galesic, Bruine de Bruin, Dumas, Kapteyn, Darling & Meijer, Nature Human Behaviour, 2018
